fixed_answer: `.html` files are supported as Astro HTML components, but they must contain only valid HTML — template expressions, imports, and frontmatter are ignored, so expressions render as literal text. fixed_answer:
`memoryCache()` is a runtime provider: responses are stored in-process in an LRU map inside your server instance (default `max: 1000` entries, evicting least-recently-used), so hits are served from that process's memory — it's explicitly suited only to single-instance deployments.

A CDN provider (`cacheNetlify()`, `cacheVercel()`, `cacheCloudflare()`) stores nothing in your server. It implements `setHeaders()` to translate cache directives into platform headers (`Netlify-CDN-Cache-Control`, `Vercel-Cache-Tag`, etc.), which are stripped before reaching the client; the CDN edge serves hits directly, without invoking your server function.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/cache-provider-reference/

issues: Conflates StaticPaths API behavior with getStaticPaths() function errors; NoMatchingStaticPathFound and InvalidGetStaticPathsReturn are getStaticPaths() errors, not StaticPaths API errors
fixed_answer: Don't use the `StaticPaths` API (added in `astro@6.0.0`) to generate page routes — it exists for adapters collecting prerender paths from within their target runtime (e.g. `workerd`), not for page code; use `getStaticPaths()` for that. It only has a real implementation in the `prerender` Vite environment, so elsewhere it is a no-op and yields no paths. Missing paths in an adapter's prerender step mean those pages won't be prerendered.

issues: Describes Starlight authoring conventions, not Astro 7 core content authoring; Astro 7 uses content collections (defineCollection, glob loaders) for Markdown/MDX, not raw files
fixed_answer: Author content as Markdown or MDX files in a content collection. Define a collection in `src/content.config.ts` using `defineCollection()` with a `type: 'content'` loader (glob-based), then query it via `getCollection()` or `getEntry()` in your pages. Frontmatter is typed via the collection schema. No headless CMS required.

issues: Conflates plain markdown frontmatter (no TS validation) with content collections (schema validation). The tutorial uses plain markdown; `InvalidContentEntryFrontmatter` is legacy (removed v6), but new content collections (v3+) do validate via zod schemas.
fixed_answer: For plain Markdown files (like the tutorial), Astro does not validate frontmatter at compile time — use optional chaining at runtime: `post.frontmatter.tags?.map(...)`. With content collections (Astro 7), define a schema in `src/content/config.ts` using `zod`; TypeScript then validates frontmatter against the schema in your editor. The `InvalidContentEntryFrontmatter` error shown in legacy docs applies only to the v1–v5 content collections API removed in Astro 6.

issues: trySerializeLocals returns string | undefined (not throw) on failure; use case is specifically for serializing locals for edge-to-serverless handoff
fixed_answer: Use `trySerializeLocals` in an Astro integration when you need to serialize `Astro.locals` to a string, such as when passing locals from edge middleware to a serverless function for rendering. It returns the serialized string if successful, or `undefined` if the value cannot be serialized (it does not throw). Import it from `astro/middleware` (added in `astro@2.8.0`).

Claims handler-side auth 'runs after the action executes'; never addresses the asked `context.locals.user` angle
fixed_answer: Middleware runs before the action handler: `getActionContext(context)` in `onRequest` exposes `action.calledFrom`, so you can gate calls (e.g. reject RPC requests when `context.locals.user` is unset) before `action.handler()` is ever invoked, and distinguish RPC from form submissions. Authorization written inside the action handler only runs once that handler is called, so it cannot pre-filter requests. Middleware can also persist results via `setActionResult()` and `serializeActionResult()`.

fixed_answer: Yes, technically: Astro middleware's `onRequest(context, next)` runs for every on-demand request, so you can read signature headers from `context.request.headers` and verify the Web Bot Auth HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421) before rendering, rejecting unsigned or invalid requests. In practice, Web Bot Auth verification is expected at the edge/CDN layer ("Let the edge do it"), which validates signatures before traffic reaches your app, so middleware verification is a fallback rather than the primary check.

unsupported claim: foreground astro dev prints info and exits; docs say it errors without --ignore-lock (--background is what prints info and exits)
fixed_answer: The already-running background server keeps running and its lock file (`.astro/dev.json`) stays in place — `ASTRO_DEV_BACKGROUND=0` only affects the command you are starting now. That new `astro dev` runs in the foreground, but because a lock file already exists for the project it does not start a second server: Astro detects the conflict and errors instead of starting another instance. To run a server alongside the existing one, use `astro dev --ignore-lock --port 4322`; to replace it, run `astro dev --background --force`, which stops the running server and starts a new one.

issues: docs say set()/tags/options log a warning and invalidate() throws when no provider is configured (not silent no-ops), and recommend guarding with cache.enabled rather than saying conditional checks are unnecessary
fixed_answer:
Caching never happens in `astro dev`: `cache.enabled` is always `false` in development mode, so responses are not stored even though the call itself does nothing harmful. When no cache provider is configured, `cache.set()`, `cache.tags`, and `cache.options` log a warning and `cache.invalidate()` throws an error, so guard caching logic with `if (Astro.cache.enabled) { ... }`. To test caching locally, configure a provider in `astro.config.mjs` (e.g. `cache: { provider: memoryCache() }`, with `memoryCache` imported from `astro/config`), then run `astro build` and serve the result with `astro preview`.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/caching/

closing sentence miscasts client:load as 'deferring' hydration; it hydrates immediately on page load
fixed_answer: `server:defer` keeps rendering on the server: the component's content is rendered on-demand on the server (deferred until its contents are available) and fetched into the page as HTML, without delaying the rest of the page's render. `client:load` keeps initial rendering on the server too — the component first renders to static HTML — but then sends its JavaScript (and the UI framework's JavaScript) to the browser, where it hydrates immediately on page load and becomes interactive. In short: `server:defer` defers server-side rendering per component (server island), while `client:load` hydrates the component in the browser as soon as the page loads.

issues: Doesn't mention Astro's `is:inline` behavior — adding `integrity` attribute triggers `is:inline`, skipping bundling/optimization
fixed_answer: Add `integrity` (SHA-256/384/512 hash) and `crossorigin="anonymous"` to the `<script>` tag. In Astro, any attribute besides `src` implies `is:inline`, so the script won't be bundled. For external CDN scripts, reference by absolute URL in `public/` and write the `<script>` tag manually. Generate hash: `curl -s <url> | openssl dgst -sha384 -binary | openssl base64 -A`.

Generic web advice; doesn't explain how to set response headers in Astro (middleware, endpoints, or adapter config)
fixed_answer: Set the `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` header on resource responses. In Astro, use middleware (`export function onRequest()`) to add it to all responses, or set per-endpoint via `new Response(body, { headers: { 'Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy': 'same-origin' } })`. Values: `same-origin` (most restrictive), `same-site`, `cross-origin`.

issues: Invented COOP value `noopener-allow-popups`; valid values are unsafe-none, same-origin, same-origin-allow-popups, same-origin-plus-COEP
fixed_answer:
Set the `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` (COOP) response header to `same-origin` on your pages. COOP places your document in its own browsing context group and severs the `window.opener` link, so a page on another origin can no longer reach back into your tab and silently replace it with a fake login screen (tabnabbing) or probe sites the user is signed in to. Use `same-origin-allow-popups` if you must keep some opener relationships; `unsafe-none` is the default and blocks nothing.

Docs: https://specification.website/spec/security/cross-origin-isolation/

issues: kebab-case comment irrelevant to resource hints
`is:inline` is not implied by attributes; it's an explicit opt-out directive
fixed_answer: Both attributes keep the browser from stopping HTML parsing and download the script in parallel; they differ in execution timing. `defer` runs after the parser finishes, in document order, before `DOMContentLoaded`—right for your application code that depends on the DOM or on other scripts in order. `async` runs as soon as the file arrives, in arrival order, possibly mid-parse—only for self-contained third-party code like analytics. In Astro, `is:inline` is an explicit directive that tells Astro to leave the `<script>` tag as-is in the output (no bundling, no processing). When `is:inline` is used, attributes like `defer` that control loading of an external file have no effect. Since Astro 5.0, scripts render as declared—no hoisting to `<head>`, no bundling of multiple scripts—so review your tags and their attributes accordingly.

fixed_answer: Add `type: 'data'` to your collection config for a data collection. Collections are `type: 'content'` by default, so you encounter `ContentCollectionTypeMismatchError` ("COLLECTION contains EXPECTED_TYPE entries, but is configured as a ACTUAL_TYPE collection") when the entries in the collection don't match the configured type — typically data entries in a collection still configured as content, or content entries in a collection marked `type: 'data'`. Content and data entries cannot live in the same collection (`MixedContentDataCollectionError`).

issues: Does not clearly answer when to choose manual vs auto-configured; only restates the difference.
client:only components are never server-rendered, so the fallback slot claim is wrong
fixed_answer:
`client:only` skips HTML server rendering entirely and renders only in the browser, so a purely client-side component is never executed during build/SSR — avoiding failures from browser-only state or server-unavailable APIs (since Astro 6, calling `getImage()` on the client throws). Because Astro never runs the component on the server, you must pass the framework explicitly, e.g. `<SomeReactComponent client:only="react" />`. Note that `client:only` components cannot use a `fallback` slot, since nothing is rendered on the server to fall back from.
Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/

issues: Invents `sessionDrivers.redis` from `astro/config` — no built-in session drivers exist in Astro 7; you must implement a custom driver or use a community package.
fixed_answer: Astro 7 has no built-in session drivers. You must implement a custom driver (a `SessionDriverConfig` with `entrypoint`/`config` plus a runtime module implementing `setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem`), or use a community package. The driver config goes in `astro.config.mjs` under `session: { driver: myDriver({ ... }) }`. Building your own is only needed when you require custom logic like a default `ttl` or runtime config overrides. Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/session-driver-reference/

issues: Claims i18n.defaultLocale is required; it is optional in Astro (only i18n.locales is required).
fixed_answer:
The `i18n` API (the `i18n` config and `astro:i18n` module) is only relevant when you need locale-based routing of pages; it is not appropriate when you aren't building a multilingual site, or when your project structure doesn't match its requirements — `i18n.locales` is a required field, and your content folders must exactly match the configured locales. Similarly, functions like `notFound()` from `astro:i18n` are available only when `i18n.routing` is set to `"manual"`, so they don't apply to other setups. For organizing unrelated structured content rather than locales, content collections (or simple pages for a small number of pages) are the appropriate tool instead.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/configuration-reference/

issues: Near duplicate of Item 1

Starlight i18n keys mischaracterized: defaultLocale is a top-level Starlight option and root is a locales key, not fields of the locales option
fixed_answer:
Avoid Astro's i18n API when you need routing behavior its built-in options can't express: set `i18n.routing: "manual"`, which disables Astro's i18n middleware so you write your own logic with helpers like `redirectToDefaultLocale()`, `notFound()`, and `redirectToFallback()`, or run Astro's `middleware()` yourself with `sequence()`. No other `routing` options (e.g. `prefixDefaultLocale`) may be combined with `routing: "manual"`. It's also appropriate when an integration handles translations for you: Starlight configures i18n through its own top-level `defaultLocale` option and its `locales` object (`label`, `lang`, `dir`, plus a special `root` key for a language served without a URL prefix).

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/internationalization/

issues: Attributes null conversion to discriminatedUnion specifically; it's general form data behavior
fixed_answer: When using form inputs in Astro actions, an empty text field is converted to `null` instead of an empty string (`""`). This differs from arrays or booleans, which retain their original types even when empty. For example: a `<input type="text" />` with no value becomes `null`; an array input like `<input name="tags[]" type="text" multiple />` results in an empty array (`[]`) if no values are submitted; boolean inputs (e.g., checkbox) use `.coerce.boolean()` and convert to `false` or `true`, not `null`. This behavior applies to all form data, not just discriminatedUnion, and ensures validation can distinguish between explicitly provided and missing data.

Muddled claims: Astro does not 'strip out' JS, and set:html does not 'cost bytes without benefit'; sanitization is the actual XSS fix, islands only reduce JS surface. First context URL (Starlight site search) irrelevant
fixed_answer:
Avoid `set:html` when Prepr article content is untrusted or editable by non-developers: the directive injects its argument as raw HTML with no sanitization, so scripts, event handlers, or iframes stored in the CMS execute in your visitors' browsers (XSS). If you must render CMS HTML, pass it through an allowlist HTML sanitizer first; render plain-text fields as text rather than HTML.

The stronger architecture is to map Prepr's structured content blocks to Astro components instead of injecting a single raw HTML string: Astro components render to static HTML and ship no client-side JavaScript by default, so only genuinely interactive pieces need a `client:*` directive to become hydrated islands. That removes the raw-HTML injection surface entirely and keeps the shipped JavaScript proportional to the interactivity the page actually needs.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/concepts/islands/

Key edge cases when implementing a client entrypoint:

1. Listen for the `astro:unmount` event on the island's root element to tear down mounted application state when the island is removed.
2. Support `client:only` by clearing `element.innerHTML` before hydrating, since no server-rendered markup exists to reuse.
3. The hydrator's final argument includes `client`, naming the directive in use (`load`, `idle`, `visible`, `only`, ...), so you can branch behavior on it.
4. If a component uses a client directive but the renderer does not provide a `clientEntrypoint`, Astro throws a `NoClientEntrypoint` error at runtime — always pass `clientEntrypoint` to `addRenderer()` when supporting directives.

fixed_answer: `this.querySelector` searches only the descendants of that element within the same DOM tree (its light DOM children), while `document.querySelector` searches the entire document and can match markup belonging to other component instances. Note that neither crosses a shadow boundary: to search inside an element's shadow root, call `this.shadowRoot.querySelector(...)`. Prefer `this.querySelector` inside `connectedCallback` (e.g. `this.querySelector('button')`) so each instance only touches its own markup, and use `document.querySelector` only when you intentionally need an element outside the component.

fixed_answer: The `i18n.fallback` option maps a locale to another locale that supplies content for missing routes: `fallback: { fr: "es" }` makes Astro build a page in `src/pages/fr/` for every page that exists in `src/pages/es/`. Each generated page follows `i18n.routing.fallbackType`: the default `"redirect"` sends visitors from the missing `/fr/...` route to the corresponding `/es/...` route, while `"rewrite"` serves the `/es/` page's content at the originally requested `/fr/...` URL instead of a 404.

issues: Missing import for getActionContext from astro:actions
fixed_answer: Import `getActionContext` from `astro:actions` and use it in middleware to inspect action requests. In `onRequest`, call `getActionContext(context)` to retrieve the action info, then check `action?.calledFrom === "rpc"` for client-side calls. Return a `Response` (e.g., 403) to block unauthorized requests. Example: `import { getActionContext } from 'astro:actions'; export function onRequest(context, next) { const { action } = getActionContext(context); if (action?.calledFrom === 'rpc' && !context.cookies.has('user-session')) return new Response('Forbidden', { status: 403 }); return next(); }`

Misattributes the ImageMetadata behavior to Vite; Astro's asset pipeline is what makes image imports return metadata objects
fixed_answer:
Images such as `.png` are handled by Astro's asset pipeline: importing one returns an `ImageMetadata` object with `src`, `width`, `height`, and `format`, so it can be passed directly to `<Image />`. Assets that aren't images, like `.mp4`, fall through to Vite's default asset handling and return a plain URL string such as `/_astro/video.hash.mp4`, so they are never processed by the image pipeline.

Docs: https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/imports/

issues: Example rationale is inverted/confusing (Unified vs satteri processor inheritance)
fixed_answer: Set `extendMarkdownConfig: false` when `.mdx` files should not inherit any of your project's `markdown` config. With the default (`true`), MDX inherits options such as `remarkPlugins`, `rehypePlugins`, `syntaxHighlight`, and `processor`, and you override individual options on the MDX integration. With `false`, MDX ignores all project-level Markdown settings and uses only what you configure on the integration itself (including its default `satteri()` processor). This is useful, for example, when your project configures a custom `markdown.processor` for `.md` files and you want `.mdx` files to keep the default pipeline instead.
